A0038.title: Proxy Detection
A0038.definition: Detecting the use of proxies when users request network resources.
A0038.description: Proxy identification analyzes data characteristics of user requests to detect the use of network proxies and endpoint proxies, further verifying whether the request originates from a genuine user.
A0038.limitation: The primary challenge of proxy identification is that legitimate users may also use proxies (e.g., corporate egress, CDN, accelerators), which can lead to false positives and disrupt normal business operations. Fraudsters can bypass IP-based blocking by leveraging residential proxy pools and dial-up ADSL to frequently rotate IPs, while mobile carrier egress IPs are difficult to blacklist directly.

references.title: GeoIP Anonymous IP Databases: Proxy, VPN, and Anonymous Address Detection - MaxMind

A0038-001.title: Web Access Proxy Detection
A0038-001.definition: Detecting the access proxy used when users request resources (a typical access proxy is a web browser).
A0038-001.description: Black-gray industry actors may use non-standard web access proxies to request resources, such as headless browsers, curl, wget, or HTTP libraries from various programming languages. Detection methods include: User-Agent analysis, JavaScript environment detection, JA3 fingerprinting, HTTP/2 fingerprinting, etc.
A0038-001.limitation: Because web access proxy detection ultimately relies on analyzing terminal request information, placing this measure in a high-adversarial context makes it easy to bypass by forging and modifying data.

A0038-002.title: Network Proxy Detection
A0038-002.definition: Detecting whether users are using a network proxy when requesting resources.
A0038-002.description: Common network proxy methods include VPN, SOCKS5, and HTTP proxies. Current common network proxy detection methods include: IP intelligence, request IP clustering, IP attribute analysis, TCP/IP fingerprinting, DNS server location discrepancy, using WebRTC to expose the real IP, and leveraging the network latency characteristics of proxies to determine whether a network proxy is being used.
A0038-002.limitation: Network proxy detection has the following limitations: first, normal users may also use network proxies, making false positives easy; second, using mobile carrier egress IPs as proxies makes blocking difficult even when detected; third, using ADSL dial-up networks as proxies allows immediate switching to a new proxy by re-dialing after being blocked.

A0038-003.title: TLS/HTTP Fingerprinting
A0038-003.definition: Identifying the true client type via TLS handshake and HTTP/2 protocol-layer fingerprints, distinguishing real browsers from protocol crawlers and automation scripts.
A0038-003.description: TLS/HTTP fingerprinting is a technique for identifying client types based on protocol-layer characteristics. Typical fingerprints include: JA3/JA4 fingerprints (hashes computed from TLS ClientHello fields such as version, cipher suites, extensions, and elliptic curves, which can identify the client's TLS implementation library, e.g., OpenSSL, BoringSSL, or browser TLS stacks); HTTP/2 fingerprints (based on SETTINGS frame parameters, window updates, header compression dynamic table characteristics, etc., to distinguish browsers from libraries like curl or Python requests); and TCP/IP fingerprints (based on MSS, window size, TLS options, etc., to distinguish operating systems). Real browsers and protocol crawlers or automation libraries have inherent differences in protocol-layer implementation. Even if an attacker forges the User-Agent, their TLS/HTTP2 fingerprint will still reveal the true client type. This method serves as a protocol-layer supplement to browser access proxy identification based on UA and JS environment checks. It is harder to forge than User-Agent and is an important technique for identifying protocol crawlers and automation scripts, and it can also support client-consistency checks in API risk control. Note the distinction from browser access proxy detection: that measure focuses on browser proxy type identification such as headless browsers, curl, and wget, while this measure focuses on protocol fingerprints, TLS stack implementation, and HTTP/2 behavior sequences.
A0038-003.limitation: TLS fingerprints of mainstream browsers and automation tools can be deliberately aligned (e.g., by using curl-impersonate or modifying TLS library parameters to simulate browser fingerprints). JA3/JA4 fingerprint databases require continuous maintenance to cover new client versions. Some clients' fingerprints may change due to system or library upgrades, posing a risk of false positives. Intermediate layers such as CDNs and security gateways may rewrite TLS fingerprints, causing identification distortion.
